A dead engine, an empty tank, one pair of hands under the bonnet and the rest of them watching the road.
Off: no hostile factions spawn, and raids and outposts stop. Friendly, neutral and careful NPCs still spawn.

How often NPC gunfire hits players. Medium is each NPC's own aiming skill, unchanged. Very Easy is 40%% of it, Easy 65%%, Hard 125%%, Very Hard 150%%, Hardcore 180%%. Accuracy against zombies is set on the Combat page.
Scales how often NPC gunfire hits a ZOMBIE. 100 is unchanged; raise it if crews look helpless against a horde. Does not affect their aim against you.
Which profiles may keep the Infinite ammunition tick. Creator profiles only keeps it for profiles you made or edited; the shipped roster then runs dry like everyone else.
Ammo drops follow what the NPC carried
On: a body drops at most its profile's magazine limit, filled only from rounds it still carried when it died. Off: one roll per magazine the profile was issued, full, however much was fired.

The most spare rounds an NPC can carry for one gun, counted in loads of that gun (its magazine or tube, at least 6 rounds). It caps the spawn kit and ammunition the NPC picks up. 0 means no ceiling. Default 6.
Rounds an NPC is issued at spawn, as a percent of what its profile says. 100 is the profile. Every gun keeps at least one full load. Infinite-ammo profiles are not changed.

How hard NPCs work a door, a window or a barricade when they break in. 100 is the tested default: a window takes three swings, a plank four, a plain door about half a minute, and only one man swings while the rest cover him. Lower it and they take longer; raise it and they come through faster.
A round an NPC puts into a zombie goes on into the zombie standing right behind it (up to three squares). Zombies only, never people; better against a horde. Off by default.
Planked windows and doors mark a building as somebody's.
Player-built walls, gates and fences mark a location as occupied.
An active generator is strong evidence somebody is living nearby.
A running or hotwired vehicle marks the area around it as worth searching.
Scales how readily NPCs act on traces. Higher investigates weaker evidence; lower needs a stronger lead.
With nothing to fight, NPCs search areas where they notice signs of survivors.
A parked NPC nobody has been near for this many in-game hours is cleaned up. Persistent NPCs (admin anchors, encounter garrisons) never expire. 0 disables the cleanup.

How often a dead NPC's gun or melee weapon stays on the body. Per NPC profile keeps each profile's own chance from the Creator. Anything else is the chance for every NPC. A spawn from the admin spawner still uses its own row. Needs Allow weapon drops on.

What shape a dropped weapon is in. Per NPC profile keeps each profile's own rating and the early-game curve, where the first weeks mostly give you broken or nearly broken guns. Anything else is the condition of every dropped weapon, from every NPC. Broken means it has to be repaired before it works. The NPC still fights with it at full strength.
How often the Roadside Pickers turn up: small scavenging crews who warn you off and may hold you up, common in the first two weeks and gone by the fourth. 100 is the default weight, 0 turns them off.
Chance per roll for both natural spawners: the faction director rolls once per encounter check interval, the encounter director once per encounter roll interval. Default 25.
Game hours between natural hostile encounter checks.
Game minutes between encounter director rolls (sleeping and fast-forward roll too). Default 60, range 10-720. The spawn chance per roll comes from the encounter chance option.
The encounter director: patrols, raids, scavenging parties, assassination squads and garrisons rolled from the catalog near players, placed by the map's own town zones.
Groups travel together in formation rather than as separate walkers.
Scales natural group sizes. 100 keeps the authored sizes.
Hostiles walk toward gunfire, shouts and other traces they notice.
Hard cap for natural persistent hostile actors.

The conduct layer: squad leaders that deploy and rally their group, snipers that keep distance, medics that dress their wounded, ambushers that wait in the dark, stealth killers. Off disables every conduct at once.
Armed NPCs get out of the line of fire to reload, break contact when hurt, and fight from behind walls and corners.
A shooter that loses sight of its target dumps the magazine into the last known position, full auto, spraying left and right. Pistols magdump too.
After a fight, a wounded NPC stops, bandages, and loses the limp and the bleeding.
Armed NPCs keep the gun on their target, or on where it was last seen, while they walk, back off or sidestep.

A shooter that is losing breaks contact, runs about a block back, holes up out of sight -- inside a building when there is one -- then comes back in from another side. Ranged only; melee always closes.
A two-handed swing by an NPC carries into a second zombie standing in the arc, at three quarters of the blow. Zombies only, never people. Off by default.

How likely a squad is to keep moving and working after dark. The rest find a house for the night or make a camp: they draw the curtains, hang sheets over the windows, sit tight until morning and leave the dead outside alone. No risks: everybody holes up. Risk takers: hardly anybody does.
Flashlights: NPCs carry a light and see 12 tiles in the dark (20 with the light on you). Night vision: NPCs simply see at night; give them the goggles yourself.
A squad that lost people to you and got away comes back for you two to three days later, with backup.

How many squads travel the map while nobody is near, default 18. They are kept in the save and come back after a restart up to this number; the saved group limit does not apply to them, except at 0 or in local-only mode, where it decides how many are kept. The roaming group rate scales it, and from the fourth day the world thins out to about a third by the third week. 0 turns the offline world off; encounters near players and outposts remain. A change made in game applies within a game minute: a higher number lets new squads found; a lower one, or 0, founds none and the squads already out keep moving until the next load, which retires the extra ones.
How often offline squads move and decide.
How far an offline squad walks in one in-game hour. Default 150, a walking pace at the default day length; towns are 1700-3400 tiles apart.
Minimum time between new offline parties, default 1.5; the offline squad cap still applies.
Simultaneous patrol, scavenging or hunting teams from each outpost. Default 2, at most 4; zero disables dispatches. Crews are session-only; the site remains saved.
A proposed outpost is built only while a player is this close (so the ground is loaded), and never within 40 tiles of anyone.
The chance each roll founds a new outpost.
Fortified stations, held houses and forest camps appear over time, manned by a garrison that never leaves.
How often the world rolls for a new outpost, in game minutes (sleeping and fast-forward roll too). A world whose clock stands still falls back to the same number of real minutes.
How many outposts may stand at the same time. 0 turns them off.
Camps and field bases outside towns (max)
How many outdoor sites -- forest camps, field bases, aid stations, depots -- may stand at once, on top of the per-town limit for fortified buildings. 0 disables outdoor sites.
How many outposts one town may hold.
A built outpost is manned when a player comes this close.
Relative frequency of natural 4+ person groups. Default is one group for every three lone parties.
Relative frequency of natural 1–3-person parties. Faction overrides take priority.
Patrols and scout parties stop off the road every few hours and after a fight: a circle, one sits, one smokes, the rest drink and talk, then the route resumes.
Game hours between scheduled rests, per squad, with some jitter. A rest after a fight comes on its own.
The longest rest, in game minutes.
The shortest rest, in game minutes.

How many groups are written into the save and come back after a restart, default 20. It counts outpost garrisons and crews an admin or an encounter made persistent. Offline squads are not counted: they come back up to the offline squad limit. Residents of places manned at the start are saved with their buildings and not counted either. Everyone else lasts the current session. Lowering it leaves the extra groups out of the next save, never removing anyone in front of you; a change made in game applies within a game minute.
The most places in the whole world that Populate places on start may man, default 45. The places are chosen once per world; the heaviest (stations, fire houses, clinics) are kept first.

Once per world, the towns' rooms are read and a share of the places a survivor would hold -- police stations, fire houses, clinics and the dentist, gun stores, warehouses, gas stations, motels, diners, churches, schools, stores and houses -- are marked to be manned: Rare 10%%, Uncommon 20%%, Common 35%% of them, every town at least two. A marked place gets its residents the first time a player comes near, from a faction that fits the room: police in the station, the fire department in the fire house, hospital staff on the ward, a family in a house. They are persistent and saved with the world. Off by default; Realistic outbreak does not turn it on.
Scales the global encounter gate. 100 is the balanced default.
Deserted -- almost nobody left (lightest on FPS)
Sparse -- a few lone survivors (light on FPS)
Balanced -- the tested default, moderate FPS cost (no change)
Crowded -- groups, outposts and frequent raids (heavy on FPS)
Insane -- past the tested limits, unsupported (will cost frames)

IF THE GAME STUTTERS, TURN THIS DOWN FIRST. Everything this mod costs in frame time comes from how many people the world is carrying, and this one setting decides that. The default is deliberately on the generous side so a new world feels inhabited; drop it one step and the county is still populated but noticeably cheaper. Rough guide on a mid-range machine: Deserted and Sparse are close to free, Balanced is the level everything is tested at, Crowded asks real work of a weaker CPU, and Insane is a stress test rather than a way to play. A dedicated server feels every step harder than singleplayer, because it simulates for everyone at once. One knob for every number below it. It sets how many survivors the world carries, how many towns are manned at the start, how often you meet them, whether they travel alone or in groups, how many outposts stand, when raids start and how far apart they are, and how large a raid wave, a scout party or a backup call is. Balanced is the tested default and writes nothing at all, so an existing save keeps every number it already has. Any option you set yourself still wins: the preset only moves options left at their own default, so tune one slider and the preset will not touch it -- the one thing it cannot see is you deliberately choosing the value that was already the default (for the four limits below, also the default of an older version). Offline squads, saved groups, outpost task squads and manned places never go below their defaults on Deserted or Sparse, so a quieter preset never removes anyone from a world already under way; Crowded and Insane raise them, Insane to 60 offline squads (default 18) and 4 task squads per outpost (default 2). Changed during a game, the preset moves only the offline squad and saved group limits until the next load. Insane deliberately goes past the mod's own hard caps: up to 220 live hostiles (tested ceiling 120), 24 outposts (12), 4 per town (2), 12 outdoor camps (6) and 8-strong scout parties (3). It is not tested at those numbers -- expect a heavier server, expect bugs, and back up your save first.
Allows your profession to change NPC attitudes, including profession rules set in the Creator. Off by default. Faction and folder relations still apply.
A survivor-run station with scanner traffic, military chatter, call-ins, stories, jokes and rumours about what is really happening in your world.

Default 99600 = 99.6 MHz. Choose an unused FM frequency if the emergency station or another mod already occupies it. The station never replaces another channel. Restart the server after changing this; open a radio to add the matching preset.

Chance to start the scout-led buildup on each check (every 10 game minutes by default). The default 0.02 with a 14-day cooldown means about one full-scale raid every six or seven weeks. 0 turns automatic raids off.
How often the raid director checks automatic eligibility.
Minimum time between automatic full-scale raids.
Automatic raids require a successfully spawned enemy scout party, buildup time, and the minimum day. The admin panel can force a raid.
Requested attackers in each wave. Spawn admission still enforces runtime limits.
Every A-Life helicopter: raid and reinforcement drops, night searchlights and flyovers. Off means none of them fly.
Automatic raids cannot begin before this world-age day.
Wait this long after scouts successfully arrive before a raid can start.
An expired scout report cannot authorize a raid; new scouts must be sent.
Number of enemy scouts sent before an automatic full-scale raid.
Paces reinforcement waves after the initial warning.
Number of attacking waves per raid.
How often the encounter director rolls a new group near players. Low halves the chance, Abundant triples it (the roll interval is unchanged).
How many groups the world keeps: the spawn multiplier and the offline squad cap together. Low halves both, Abundant triples them (within their own ceilings).
Distant gunfire, helicopters, car crashes and the world's ambience: Low halves the daily and weekly caps and doubles the gap between events, Abundant triples the caps and shortens the gap.
How often the factions that are friendly or neutral to the player are picked when a group is founded. Low halves their weight against the hostile ones, Abundant triples it.

The first days of the outbreak, the way they would go. The National Guard holds a checkpoint on the bridge north of West Point, and the first three days bring more of everything. After day 3 the police and the army are gone from the roads for good; the bridge checkpoint is abandoned after 72 hours and everything it placed is removed. On by default.
Members that fall behind close back up on their group instead of drifting.
Scales how often an outlaw crew chooses to rob instead of fighting. 100 is normal, 0 never, 200 twice as often.
Outlaw crews may hold up a lone player instead of shooting: hands up, the weapon down, three or four valuable items taken, then they leave. Refuse, and they shoot.
Extra no-spawn tiles around multiplayer safehouses.
Maximum distance for selecting a nearby building; larger values increase search work.
Maximum collected items before heading back to the camp/base depot.
Bring supplies home after searching this many buildings.
Hostile looters may take nearby supplies.
An NPC that spots something tells its group where, once. Not a live feed.
Shouting draws every NPC within earshot toward you.
NPCs walk to where a target was last seen and sweep the area before giving up.
Winter adds coats, hats, gloves and scarves to empty slots; summer takes off heavy winter layers. Uniforms keep their uniform. Profiles with their own seasonal outfit sets are left as authored.
Show admin tools in the right-click menu
The spawn panel, encounter list, outpost builder and raid setup. Turn this off for a clean right-click menu; Runtime status and the Creator stay either way. Admins on a server are unaffected.
Distance in tiles at which persistent actors receive physical shells.
Allows sprint windows for melee closing, cover moves, and retreats. Off keeps those moves at a run or walk.
A squad in contact may call a quick-reaction squad; limited calls, a cooldown, and a real chance of no answer.
Chance of a permitted support call succeeding.
Minimum game time between successful calls by the same group.
Fallback when the caller/faction has no authored support size.
Duration of the virtual support helicopter presentation.
Limits repeated reinforcement requests from one group.
Chance for an authorized helicopter spotlight call. Ground-only callers cannot use it.
Follows the target player while outdoors; goes dark indoors.
Type in chat near NPCs and they answer: questions, requests, threats, yes or no. They also react with words when you hit them or help them in a fight.
Friendly and neutral people stop and look at you when you come close and say something; friends passing by say a word; outlaw crews call out a stranger.
Scared ordinary people do not open fire on someone who has not attacked them, and back off when they are badly outgunned. Veterans and predators never do.
Single player has no chat window. With this on, the Toggle chat key opens a small line to talk to NPCs. Start a line with ! to shout it.
Draws a visible streak along each shot an NPC fires. Muzzle flash, gunfire and casings are unaffected either way.
A moving vehicle hurts an NPC it hits, scaled by speed. Turn this off to stop the vehicle check running at all. NPCs still cannot reach you through an intact car window either way.
Plays recorded voice clips for what NPCs say. Off by default: NPCs talk in text only. Pain and death sounds are not affected.
Allows hostile A-Life factions to fight one another.
Eligible NPC weapons may survive into corpse inventory.
Base chance per trigger pull for a non-revolver NPC firearm to jam. Zero disables jams even if the feature is enabled.
Non-revolver NPC firearms can fail to fire, click, then be visibly racked clear.
Full A-Life (offline squads roam the map)
Local only (groups near players; outposts stay)

Full: squads roam the whole map while nobody is near (offline simulation) and appear when you get close; outposts rise and fall on their own. Local only: no offline squads -- NPC groups exist only near players (cheapest); outposts still rise.
Hits mark NPCs: a leg wound takes their run away, and below ten percent health they bleed out in seconds unless they bandage.
